title: Annual vegetables in an establishing forest garden
subtitle: Using the open ground between young trees for annual food crops while the system establishes.
excerpt: In the first three to five years of a forest garden, the open ground between young trees is too valuable to leave bare. Annual vegetables fill this space productively while the woody plants establish, and they provide a return from the plot while waiting for the perennial system to mature.
sourceNotes: Annual integration strategy from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). No-dig approach to annual growing from Charles Dowding, No Dig Organic Home and Garden (2013).

glossaryTerms.definition: A fast-growing annual crop grown between slow-establishing perennials to cover the ground, suppress weeds, and provide yield while the permanent planting establishes. The nurse crop is removed or incorporated as the perennials grow to fill the space.

content.text: Annual vegetables grown between young trees and shrubs act as
. They cover the soil, suppress weeds, and provide food while the permanent planting establishes.

Choose crops that do not need a permanent structure or deep root disturbance. Squash, courgette, and pumpkin are good: they cover the ground with leaves and ask little. Beans (runner and French) fix nitrogen and leave the soil richer. Salads and root vegetables fill gaps between larger crops.

Keep annual crops at least 1 m from the base of newly planted trees. Do not dig near tree roots. Use a no-dig approach: top-dress with compost and plant directly into it. Annual crops should occupy the open spaces and leave a mulched circle around each tree untouched.

As trees and shrubs establish, they cast more shade and take up more root space. Annual crops become less productive in these conditions. From year four or five, the annual growing space shrinks and perennial ground cover and herbaceous plants take over. This is the intended process: do not try to maintain annual crops indefinitely.
